q: Two websites repeat the same unreferenced claim. What best strengthens verification?
options: Count reposts as independent confirmation
Trace the claim to original evidence and check independent credible sources
Choose the more attractive website
Accept it if it is recent
explanation: Repeated claims may share one source; provenance and independent evidence matter.

q: A chart omits its denominator and collection period. What should you do before using it?
options: Find the underlying dataset, definitions and time coverage
Quote the chart without qualification
Infer the denominator from colours
Assume all percentages refer to the same population
explanation: Definitions, denominators and dates determine whether a comparison is valid.

q: You need the current legal text rather than an old commentary. What is the strongest starting point?
options: A cached personal blog
A social-media screenshot
An official legal database with version and date information
The highest-ranked sponsored result
explanation: Authoritative provenance and version information help identify applicable texts.

q: A spreadsheet sorts only its first column while other columns remain fixed. What is the main risk?
options: Only the visual font changes
All formulas become more accurate
The file becomes encrypted
Values become associated with the wrong records
explanation: Sort complete records or a properly defined table to preserve relationships.

q: Two datasets use different date formats. What should precede merging them?
options: Sort each by filename only
Delete all dates
Standardise and validate the date fields
Convert every date into free-text commentary
explanation: Consistent field formats and validation prevent incorrect matching.

q: An exported CSV opens with leading zeros missing from identifiers. What is best?
options: Add a random zero to every row
Round all identifiers
Replace identifiers with row numbers
Import identifier columns as text and verify against the original
explanation: Identifiers are labels, not quantities; text import preserves leading zeros.

q: What is the best way to make a dataset reproducible?
options: Keep source, extraction date, definitions and transformation steps
Remove all metadata
Retain only the final screenshot
Rename every column to data
explanation: Provenance and documented transformations allow others to check the result.

q: A search produces mostly irrelevant results. What is the best adjustment?
options: Disable all source evaluation
Refine key terms and filters to match the information need
Accept the first result regardless
Repeat the same query indefinitely
explanation: Searching is iterative: adjust terms, context and filters.

q: Several colleagues need to edit a document. Which workflow best reduces conflicting copies?
options: Email separate copies for every edit
Remove version history
Use an approved shared document with permissions and version history
Use a public anonymous link for confidential drafts
explanation: Controlled co-authoring avoids parallel unsynchronised copies.

q: An external reviewer only needs to read one file. What access is proportionate?
options: Give administrator access
Grant named read-only access to that file
Make the entire drive public
Share another employee’s login
explanation: Least-privilege sharing limits access to the task.

q: You must email unrelated external recipients without disclosing their addresses to each other. Which field helps?
options: BCC
Subject
CC
Reply-to
explanation: BCC conceals recipients from other recipients; also follow organisational mailing rules.

q: A collaborative draft contains an edit you disagree with. What is best?
options: Silently delete everyone else’s work
Publish the dispute publicly
Send passwords to resolve the issue
Use comments or tracked changes to explain the proposed revision
explanation: Structured feedback preserves traceability and supports collaboration.

q: A meeting participant cannot hear the audio. What is the most inclusive immediate response?
options: Continue without acknowledging the issue
Provide captions or an accessible text channel and check their needs
Tell them to guess from slides
Disable the chat
explanation: Use an alternative communication channel suited to the participant’s needs.

q: A file link stops working after staff turnover. What is the best preventive practice?
options: Share account passwords
Use only temporary chat attachments
Store team records in approved team-owned locations with managed access
Store everything in one person’s private account
explanation: Organisational ownership and access management support continuity.

q: A social-media post from your account is misleading. What is the responsible response?
options: Assume deleting it erases every copy
Create fake accounts to support it
Blame an unrelated colleague
Correct it transparently and assess what information was exposed
explanation: Digital identity management includes accountability and awareness that copies may persist.

q: Which message best suits a busy non-specialist audience?
options: A clear purpose, concise request and relevant context
A subject line unrelated to the content
Unexplained acronyms and no action requested
A large unlabelled attachment only
explanation: Adapt the medium and wording to the audience and purpose.

q: A document must be navigable by screen-reader users. Which approach helps most?
options: Use colour alone for structure
Use semantic headings and meaningful reading order
Convert all text into an image
Make headings bold visually but leave all text in one paragraph
explanation: Semantic structure enables assistive navigation.

q: A chart carries essential information. What should accompany it?
options: A meaningful text alternative describing its message and relevant data
A filename as its only description
An unrelated decorative caption
No description if colours are attractive
explanation: Accessible alternatives convey the information rather than merely naming the picture.

q: A photograph is online without a reuse licence. What should you assume?
options: Every online image is public domain
Commercial reuse is always permitted
Public availability alone does not grant permission to reuse it
Attribution always replaces permission
explanation: Check copyright, permission, licence and applicable exceptions before reuse.

q: A work is licensed for non-commercial use only. What should you check before using it in a commercial campaign?
options: Only whether the file is high resolution
Whether you can remove the watermark
Whether the author has followers
Whether additional permission is required
explanation: Licence conditions constrain permitted reuse.

q: When copying a spreadsheet formula, you need the tax-rate cell to remain fixed. Which reference fits?
options: C2
B2
B1
explanation: The dollar signs lock both column and row in common A1-style spreadsheets.

q: A spreadsheet must count rows meeting a specified condition. Which function type is most appropriate?
options: A print-preview command
A password-reset command
A font-formatting command
A conditional counting function such as COUNTIF
explanation: Conditional counting evaluates records against a criterion.

q: A simple script processes each record once. Which control structure fits?
options: A command that deletes the dataset
A manual copy-and-paste for every future record
A loop over the records
A single instruction that never references the records
explanation: Loops express repeated processing systematically.

q: You adapt several sources into one report. What must you preserve?
options: All sources’ hidden tracking codes
Accurate attribution and applicable licence conditions
Only the original colours
No source information
explanation: Integration does not remove attribution or licence responsibilities.

q: An unexpected email asks you to sign in through an urgent link. What should you do first?
options: Forward your password for confirmation
Enter credentials to see what happens
Verify through a trusted independent channel rather than use the link
Disable security alerts
explanation: Independent verification avoids relying on potentially deceptive links.

q: Which account protection is strongest among these choices?
options: A short password with security alerts disabled
A unique strong password plus multi-factor authentication
A password shared in a team chat
One password reused everywhere
explanation: Unique credentials reduce reuse risk; MFA adds a separate barrier.

q: You receive an MFA approval request you did not initiate. What should you do?
options: Approve to stop the notifications
Share the one-time code publicly
Disable MFA permanently
Deny it and report it through the approved security channel
explanation: Unexpected authentication requests may indicate attempted compromise.

q: A laptop containing work data is lost. What should happen promptly?
options: Report it through organisational incident procedures
Wait several weeks
Post the device password online
Assume a login password eliminates all risk
explanation: Timely incident response enables containment and any necessary follow-up.

q: A ransomware incident encrypts active files. What is most useful for recovery?
options: A larger monitor
A list of file colours
A tested backup isolated from the affected environment
Only an automatically synchronised copy exposed to the same changes
explanation: Backups must be recoverable and protected against the same incident.

q: A colleague proposes entering personal case files into an unapproved public AI tool. What is best?
options: Do not upload them; use approved tools and assess confidentiality and data protection
Remove the filename but keep all personal details
Assume AI tools cannot retain information
Upload first and seek permission later
explanation: Tool approval, data minimisation and confidentiality remain necessary.

q: Which statement about HTTPS is correct?
options: It prevents all phishing
It makes passwords unnecessary
It guarantees the seller is honest
It protects the connection but does not prove every claim on the site is true
explanation: Encrypted transport is different from trustworthiness of content or operator.

q: Which practice supports sustainable device use when security and functional needs can still be met?
options: Dispose of batteries in general waste
Repair and extend useful life before responsible recycling
Replace working devices monthly
Disable every security update
explanation: Consider device lifecycle and responsible disposal alongside safety requirements.

q: A videoconference has no sound. What is the best initial diagnostic step?
options: Reinstall the operating system immediately
Delete all documents
Publish the meeting password
Check mute, selected audio device and a simple audio test
explanation: Start with low-risk checks of likely causes.

q: An application repeatedly fails after a recent change. What helps isolate the cause?
options: Delete unrelated accounts
Ignore error messages
Record the error and reproduce it while checking recent changes systematically
Change every setting at once
explanation: Controlled testing and evidence help locate faults.

q: A team needs a tool for confidential collaborative work. What should drive selection?
options: Requirements, approved security controls, accessibility and collaboration needs
Whether it bypasses all access checks
Only the brightest interface
Only the number of social-media mentions
explanation: Select technology against the actual needs and constraints.

q: A user struggles to read small text in an application. Which response is appropriate?
options: Tell them not to use the service
Adjust accessible display settings and check the result with the user
Reduce contrast further
Remove all labels
explanation: Customise the environment to the user’s access needs.

q: An automated workflow sends a message twice for each record. What is a sensible investigation?
options: Increase the number of triggers
Inspect trigger conditions, duplicate inputs and execution logs
Assume the recipients caused it
Delete all audit logs
explanation: Trace the workflow to distinguish duplicate data from duplicate execution.

q: A team is unsure whether staff can use a new system. What is best?
options: Assess specific skill gaps and provide targeted practice and support
Assume age determines competence
Remove all training
Treat a single self-rating as conclusive
explanation: Identify actual competence needs and support development.

q: An AI-generated summary contains a precise legal claim. What should you do before relying on it?
options: Remove the citation and publish
Trust it because it is fluent
Verify it against the authoritative original text
Treat repetition as proof
explanation: Fluency is not evidence; generated content requires verification.

q: You propose automating a repetitive approval task. What should happen before deployment?
options: Skip testing because automation is always accurate
Give the tool unrestricted permissions
Delete the manual procedure before validation
Map the process, test on controlled cases and retain appropriate human oversight
explanation: Responsible improvement includes testing, risk controls and oversight.

q: You need web results that contain the exact phrase “reserve list” and not just the individual words. What should you do?
options: Type the words in capital letters
Add the word ‘only’ before the phrase
Put the phrase in quotation marks
Separate the words with commas
explanation: Quotation marks make most search engines treat the words as one exact phrase.

q: An unfamiliar website makes a striking health claim. What is the best way to judge its credibility?
options: Check who is responsible for the content, its date and its sources, and compare with independent reliable sources
Trust it if it appears first in search results
Trust it if the page looks professional
Trust it if many people have shared it
explanation: Credibility depends on authorship, evidence and corroboration; ranking, design and popularity are not evidence.

q: You manage hundreds of project files. Which practice makes them easiest to find and avoids confusion between versions?
options: Saving everything on the desktop with short names
Naming files by the day of the week
Keeping only the newest version and deleting all others immediately
A consistent folder structure and file naming convention, for example with dates and version numbers
explanation: Consistent structure and naming make retrieval and version control predictable.

q: What is a key advantage of CSV files for exchanging tabular data between applications?
options: They always preserve cell colours and formulas
They are plain text and can be read by almost any data tool
They are encrypted by default
They can only be opened by one spreadsheet program
explanation: CSV stores values as plain text separated by delimiters; it does not store formatting or formulas.

q: You must share a confidential draft with five colleagues who need to comment on it. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Send the file as an attachment to a large mailing list
Post the file on a public website with a hard-to-guess link
Share a link with restricted access in the organisation’s approved file-sharing tool, giving only those five people permission to comment
Copy the text into a chat group that includes external guests
explanation: Restricted sharing limits access, keeps one master version and allows revocation.

q: You send an announcement to many external recipients who do not know one another. Which e-mail field should you use for their addresses?
options: Bcc, so that recipients cannot see each other’s addresses
To, so that everyone can reply easily
Cc, so that everyone is informed
The subject line
explanation: Bcc protects recipients’ privacy, which is also a data-protection concern.

q: In the EU legal framework for electronic identification and trust services (eIDAS), what is a qualified electronic signature?
options: A scanned image of a handwritten signature
A typed name at the end of an e-mail
A password-protected PDF
An electronic signature with the same legal effect as a handwritten signature
explanation: Qualified electronic signatures have the equivalent legal effect of handwritten signatures and are recognised across the EU.

q: You want to reuse a photograph from the web in a public presentation. What should you check first?
options: Whether the image resolution is high
The licence or copyright terms and any attribution requirement
Whether the picture has a watermark
Whether it is the first result in an image search
explanation: Reuse depends on the licence, for example a Creative Commons licence with attribution.

q: Why should you add alternative text to images in a document?
options: To make the file smaller
To protect the image from copying
So that people using screen readers receive the information the image conveys
To change the image’s colours automatically
explanation: Alternative text is a basic accessibility feature.

q: What is the advantage of using built-in heading styles instead of manually enlarging text?
options: The text is automatically translated
The document is protected against editing
Spelling errors are corrected automatically
The structure is machine-readable, enabling navigation, an automatic table of contents and better accessibility
explanation: Heading styles define a document structure that tools and assistive technologies can use.

q: In a spreadsheet, you copy a formula that must always refer to the same cell, A1. Which reference should you use?
options: A1
explanation: Absolute references with dollar signs remain fixed when the formula is copied.

q: You receive an urgent e-mail apparently from your bank asking you to click a link and confirm your password. What is the best action?
options: Click the link but only enter part of the password
Do not click; open the bank’s official website yourself or call a known number, and report the message
Reply to the sender asking whether it is genuine
Forward the e-mail to colleagues as a warning with the link intact
explanation: This is a typical phishing pattern. Use independent channels and report it.

q: What is the main benefit of multi-factor authentication?
options: It makes passwords unnecessary
It encrypts all e-mails automatically
It speeds up logging in
An attacker who has stolen the password still lacks the second factor
explanation: A second factor, such as an app code or security key, reduces the risk of account takeover.

q: What is the main advantage of using a password manager?
options: Passwords no longer need to be changed after a data breach
It prevents all phishing attacks
You can use long, unique passwords for each service without memorising them
It lets you share one password across all accounts safely
explanation: Unique passwords limit the damage if one service is compromised.

q: You must access your work e-mail from a public Wi-Fi network. Which is the most appropriate precaution?
options: Turn off the device’s firewall to improve speed
Use the organisation’s approved VPN or secure connection
Disable updates to avoid interruptions
Use a shared computer without logging out
explanation: A VPN encrypts traffic between your device and the organisation, reducing risks on untrusted networks.

q: You need to convert 500 scanned pages into text that can be searched and edited. Which technology is most appropriate?
options: Optical character recognition (OCR)
Data compression
Screen mirroring
A spell checker
explanation: OCR recognises characters in images and converts them to machine-readable text.

q: An online collaboration service suddenly stops working for many colleagues. What is a sensible first step?
options: Check the provider’s official service-status page and the organisation’s IT notices
Reinstall the operating system
Delete your account and create a new one
Wait a week before doing anything
explanation: Status pages and IT notices help determine whether the problem is a known outage rather than a local fault.

q: You must find a meeting time for ten colleagues in different time zones. Which tool is most suitable?
options: A group phone call to negotiate each slot
A scheduling poll or shared calendar that shows availability
An e-mail chain with all replies in one thread
A printed timetable posted in the office
explanation: Scheduling tools automate the comparison of availability and handle time zones.

q: You repeat the same formatting steps on dozens of documents every week. What is the most efficient approach?
options: Do it manually but faster
Ask colleagues to format their own documents
Create a template or automate the steps with macros or a built-in automation feature
Stop formatting the documents
explanation: Templates and automation reduce repetitive manual work and errors.

q: A team needs to keep track of who is responsible for which task on a shared project and by when. Which tool is most suitable?
options: A personal notebook kept by each team member
Private text messages between individual colleagues
A printed list that one person updates weekly
A shared task board or project-management tool with assignees and deadlines
explanation: A shared board gives everyone the same current view of tasks, owners and deadlines.
